item.title: World shares retreat as report of damage to oil tankers pushes oil prices higher
item.description: World shares and U.S. futures retreated on Thursday as oil prices jumped more than 2 per cent following a report by Iran’s state television that seven oil tankers caught fire and were damaged in the ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: World shares and U.S. futures retreated on Thursday as oil prices jumped more than 2 per cent following a report by Iran’s state television that seven oil tankers caught fire and were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz. If the report is verified, it would be the largest number of vessels damaged in the waterway in a single day since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28. Brent crude, the international standard, gained 3.2 per cent to US$112.27 per barrel. It has been bouncing between $97 and $112 in recent days on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal. U.S. benchmark crude rose 2.8 per cent to $99.80 per barrel. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX shed 1.1 per cent to 25,367.96, while the CAC 40 in Paris declined 1.3 per cent to 7,816.67. Britain’s FTSE 100 was down 0.7 per cent at 10,678.67. The future for the S&P 500 lost 1 per cent and that for the Dow Jones Industrial Average was 0.7 per cent lower. In Asia, Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 lost 2.7 per cent to 62,907.84 on heavy selling of big tech companies like SoftBank Group, which lost 6.9 per cent. Computer chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron fell 7 per cent and testing equipment maker Advantest lost 6 per cent. In South Korea, the Kospi dropped 3.5 per cent, to 5,533.77. Big memory chipmakers led the decline, with Samsung Electronics down 4 per cent. SK Hynix lost 5.5 per cent. AI stocks, at the center of market action in recent months, are under pressure from worries that construction of data centers may slow as it is becoming increasingly expensive to borrow money. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng shed 3 per cent to 22,934.68, and the Shanghai Composite index gave up 1.5 per cent to 3,658.03. Taiwan’s Taiex lost 1.8 per cent. In Australia, the S&P/ASX 200 declined 0.4 per cent to 8,793.20. The U.S. stock market rose Wednesday following strong profit reports from SpaceX, Capital One Financial and other big companies. The S&P 500 added 0.6 per cent and the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.7 per cent. The Nasdaq composite climbed 1.1 per cent. SpaceX helped lead the market and climbed 7.8 per cent after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company. Tesla rose 3.4 per cent and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500. Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 2.5 per cent, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 10.7 per cent. Expectations are high for profit growth for all kinds of companies during the summer, and they need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made despite worries about high inflation, higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street. Netflix fell 5.3 per cent even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. In other dealings early Thursday, the U.S. dollar fell to 157.22 Japanese yen from 158.14 yen late Wednesday. The euro slipped to US$1.1231 from $1.1233. Elaine Kurtenbach, The Associated Press

item.title: South African operator regains longest train record with hundreds of wagons
item.description: A South African operator set a new record for the world’s longest freight train on Monday. The 696-car, 7.6-kilometre-long train, operated by the national rail operator Transnet Freight Rail (TFR), ...
item.dc:creator: Joe Van Wonderen
item.content:encoded: A South African operator set a new record for the world’s longest freight train on Monday. The 696-car, 7.6-kilometre-long train, operated by the national rail operator Transnet Freight Rail (TFR), chugged from Saldanha to the Northern Cape on an 861-kilometre-long track, the company said on Tuesday. “The exercise was undertaken as a dynamic train evaluation programme with the dual objective of pursuing a world record and advancing technical knowledge in train design, train handling and operational performance,” according to the firm’s news release. Using electric and diesel-electric locomotives interspersed along the length of the train, the company said it was able to “operate as a synchronized unit, enabling the controlled distribution of traction and braking forces across the train’s entire length.” Australian mining company BHP previously held the world record with a train nearly seven kilometres long, according to Guinness World Records. That train consisted of 682 ore cars pushed by eight diesel-electric locomotives, set in June 2001. TFR chief executive Russell Baatjies said although the South African train ran empty, the operation “is a significant achievement.” “The real value lies in the technical knowledge and operational insights gained through this exercise,” he said. “These learnings will contribute to the continued advancement of rail operations, support innovation and strengthen our freight rail capability into the future.” The Iron Ore Export Line that TFR ran its record-setting exercise on links Sishen in the Northern Cape to Saldanha in the Western Cape. The country’s mining activity is largely concentrated north of Johannesburg and Pretoria, clustered between South Africa’s borders with Botswana, Zimbabwe and Mozambique. South Africa exported more than two million kilograms of iron products in 2024, according to the World Integrated Trade Solution. About a quarter of that went to Canada, 582,198 kilograms of product valued at approximately US$4.36 million. TFR had held the longest-train-record since 1989, before losing it to Australia.

item.title: CPP and OAS: Should you take the money or wait?: Stan Wong
item.description: Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP).
item.content:encoded:
Who would turn down a 42 per cent pay raise? That is effectively the choice facing Canadians deciding when to collect their Canada Pension Plan (CPP). Waiting until 70 rather than starting at 65 increases monthly payments by 42 per cent. The catch? Five years without collecting a penny.

Clients frequently ask me whether they should begin collecting CPP as early as age 60, wait until 65 or defer until 70, and when they should start Old Age Security (OAS). Many instinctively favour taking the money early. But the better question is how these decisions fit into their overall financial plan. Do you actually need the income? Consider two retirees, both aged 65. One has a workplace pension, substantial investments, and no immediate need for additional income. Deferring CPP could strengthen financial security later. The other relies on investment withdrawals to pay everyday expenses. Collecting earlier might reduce the need to sell investments during a market downturn. The same pension rules can produce very different answers. A comprehensive financial plan can project cash flow, compare investment withdrawals, and identify the trade-offs of waiting, including forgone returns and potential taxes. Taxes can change the calculation Both CPP and OAS are taxable, but only OAS faces an income-tested recovery tax, commonly called the clawback. For the 2026 income year, the OAS clawback starts above $95,323 in individual net income, with 15 cents recovered for each additional dollar. This generally affects recoveries from July 2027 through June 2028. At a net income of $120,000, including OAS, roughly $3,700 would be recovered. For recipients aged 65 to 74, the benefit can be fully clawed back at $155,320. CPP has no comparable clawback, although receiving it can increase taxable income and, consequently, OAS repayments. The broader retirement income picture is crucial: someone retiring before mandatory withdrawals from a registered retirement income fund (RRIF) begin may benefit from drawing down savings in a registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) during lower-income years while deferring benefits. Someone expecting substantial RRIF income later might face larger OAS clawbacks even after waiting. Coordinating pension income, registered account withdrawals and income-splitting opportunities can change which starting dates are most tax-efficient. The financial reward for waiting CPP can start at 60, with payments reduced by 36 per cent relative to 65. After 65, payments increase by 0.7 per cent for each month deferred, reaching 42 per cent at 70. OAS can start at 65. Waiting increases payments by 0.6 per cent monthly, or 36 per cent at 70. Neither benefit increases further for deferral beyond 70. Someone entitled to $1,000 monthly in CPP at 65 would receive $1,420 at 70, before future inflation adjustments. The maximum monthly OAS payment for aged 65 to 74 is $762.50 in late 2026. A 36 per cent increase would lift that base payment to approximately $1,037, before indexing. Both benefits are inflation-adjusted, and OAS rises automatically another 10 per cent at 75. How long must you live to come out ahead? Delaying $1,000 monthly in CPP from 65 to 70 means forgoing $60,000, then receiving an additional $420 monthly. On a simple cumulative-payment basis, the higher benefit catches up near age 82. For OAS, the comparable break-even is around age 83, accounting for the 10 per cent increase at 75 applicable to both starting ages. Taxes, inflation, and investment returns can change these results. According to the Office of the Chief Actuary’s 32nd CPP report , a Canadian man aged 65 in 2025 is projected to live another 21.6 years, reaching approximately age 87; for women, the projection is 24.1 years, reaching approximately age 89. These averages cannot predict individual outcomes. Health, lifestyle, and family history should inform longevity assumptions. For those who live into their 90s, higher inflation-adjusted benefits may reduce pressure on portfolios later in life. Individuals eligible for the Guaranteed Income Supplement should generally not defer OAS because doing so delays access to that supplement. A total wealth planning decision There is no universally correct age to begin CPP or OAS. Spouses may benefit from different starting dates, and taking one benefit earlier while deferring the other may make sense. Before deciding, Canadians should prepare or update a comprehensive financial plan that models different scenarios for income needs, tax exposure, portfolio sustainability, and estate objectives. The goal is not simply to collect sooner or secure the largest monthly cheque. It is to make these decisions within a broader total wealth plan that supports after-tax income and lasting financial security. item.title: S&P/TSX composite rises more than 200 points, while U.S. markets also gain ground
item.description: Canada’s main stock index rose more than 250 points, helped by financial and technology sectors, while U.S. stock markets also climbed higher.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index rose more than 200 points Wednesday, helped by gains in the technology sector, while U.S. markets also rose.  The S&P/TSX composite index was up 217.03 points at 36,324.99. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 360.21 points at 52,856.09. The S&P 500 index was up 44.60 points at 7,757.17, while the Nasdaq composite was up 278.04 points at 26,702.86.   The Canadian dollar traded for 71.14 cents US compared with 71.15 cents US on Tuesday. The December crude oil contract was down 67 cents US at US$97.15 per barrel. The December gold contract was up US$7.40 at US$4,150.00 an ounce. --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 21, 2026.
